extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans and researchers of television/comedy writing
extracted.subtask_description: Practices and standards for writing and running an animated television comedy (as exemplified by Al Jean's work on The Simpsons), covering authorship, collaboration, showrunning responsibilities, and creative quality goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and warmth in humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the show was largely based on humor, it had depth and warmth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jean valued episodes that combined comedy with emotional depth; seasons three and four are cited as higher-regarded because the show was given more depth during Jean's tenure. Aim for humor that also delivers warmth and substantive moments, not just jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative writing process
rubrics_metrics.description: "The principal writer [of an episode] has, at most, written 40% of the script. It's a real team effort."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing for the show is highly collaborative: multiple writers contribute to the final script. Producers and showrunners should expect and manage iterative team contributions rather than treating credited authorship as sole authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship credit reflects idea originator/first draft
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer credited in the episode's opening credits is the person that came up with the idea for the episode and wrote the first draft, even if he or she only contributed to a small part of the final script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit conventions allocate the writing credit to the idea originator and first-draft author regardless of final percentage contributed; producers and writers should understand and follow these credit norms when assigning authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showrunner ultimate responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A showrunner has the ultimate responsibility of all the processes that an episode goes through before completion, including the writing, the animation, the voice acting and the music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The showrunner must oversee and coordinate creative and production elements across departments to ensure episode quality; this is both managerial and creative leadership, not just a writing role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous multiple rewrites to improve humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Jean and Reiss did six to seven rewrites of a script in order to improve its humor; Jean said he 'kept thinking 'It's not good enough. It's not good enough.''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect extensive rewriting and revision cycles under pressure to enhance jokes and comedic timing; prioritize iterative improvement rather than settling on the first draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek fresh, original ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The hardest thing at this point is just thinking of fresh ideas. People are so on top of things that we've done before, so the challenge now is to think of an idea that's good, but hasn't been seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuing originality: writers should aim for concepts that feel new and avoid repeating gags or storylines that the audience already recognizes; novelty is an explicit creative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodes that read as cross-promotional advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Matt Groening publicly cited a crossover as 'a thirty-minute advertisement for The Critic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of crossovers or plot devices that are perceived as self-promotion for other projects; such episodes can provoke backlash and be judged negatively for seeming promotional rather than creatively justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance character/gag focus with broader storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Jean "guided the show away from its gag-heavy, Homer-centric incarnation...these are certainly brighter days for the show's long-time fans."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a balance between character-driven stories and gag-driven episodes; shifting away from one-dimensional gag focus toward broader character and thematic variety is presented as a quality improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage resources when expanding projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers were initially worried that creating a film would have a negative effect on the show, as they did not have enough crew to focus their attention on both projects. Additional writers and animators were hired so that both the show and the film could be produced at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When undertaking multiple large projects concurrently, plan staffing and resources to avoid quality loss on either effort; hiring additional personnel is an explicit mitigation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence in creative leadership despite criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Jean responded to criticism about decline by noting historical patterns of 'gone downhill' complaints and asserting that listening to such criticisms would have ended the show early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative leaders should weigh audience and critical feedback but avoid abandoning a project at early signs of negative reaction; persistence and long-term perspective can be part of sustaining a series.
